 KALAMAZOO, Mich. — Open enrollment for Medicare ends Monday, Dec. 7, 2026.
 As we enter November, the Kalamazoo County Area Agency on Aging says the deadline might seem like it's a long way off, but it's never a bad idea to start planning early.
 "Every year, plans change," Miranda Pearson, the program supervisor at the Kalamazoo County Area Agency on Aging, explained. "They change cost, copays, co-insurance. Everyone should have gotten a letter from their current insurance letting them know what their changes will be for 2027."
 There are also changes for some Medicare coverage going into 2027. Those changes can be found here .
 "I would say the majority of the time, you have to look and sit down and figure out, 'What are my drugs gonna cost next year and how do I make that change? How do I use Medicare.gov to review some of those things?'" Pearson explained, when asked what people should consider during open enrollment. "Even then, you might still have questions about what does this cover? What does that not cover? Is my x-ray included in that cost?'" She continued. "It could be pretty in-depth."
 Michigan's AARP says the in-depth process, coupled with the importance of signing up for the proper coverage, can make people going through open enrollment prime targets for scammers.
 Exploring Michigan : Allegan restaurant serves up steaks and spooky history 
 "We hear about it every year during open enrollment," Jennifer Feuerstein-DaVita, the senior associate state director for Michigan's AARP, said. "People are focused on reviewing their plans, they're looking at coverage, and because of the fact that they're very much focused on their Medicare planning right now."
 Being that focused on the process could mean your critical reasoning skills are somewhat compromised, according to Feuerstein-DaVita.
 "When a call comes in that they see is from Medicare, they aren't even thinking twice about it because they're already engrossed in this whole process. And so that doesn't raise a red flag," she explained.
 But, she says, you can't let your guard down.
 "You will never get an unsolicited phone call from Medicare," said Feuerstein-DaVita. "They will never call you out of the blue."
 That scammer on the other end of the line might ask you for your Medicare number, which Feuerstein-DaVita says is just as valuable as your social security number.
 "Once a fraudster has a person's Medicare number, they can start billing Medicare fraudulently. They can bill for tests that were never performed, equipment that was never received," Feuerstein-DaVita said. "Not only is this fraud and abuse to Medicare, but it actually can hurt the patient as well."
 "Let's say, for example, the scammer uses a stolen Medicare number to bill Medicare for wheelchairs or supplies or testing," she continued. "That has a lifetime benefit. If that beneficiary down the road needs to access those lifetime benefits and they've already been used and squandered by fraud, the benefit is no longer available. That stolen information may not affect them today, but it can definitely affect them down the road."
 If you do get a call or text that seems off or asks you for your personal information Feuerstein-DaVita says to hang up.
 'Times are Tough' : Food pantries navigate higher demand following SNAP changes 
 "What we found is that these scammers know that older adults could be going through a lot," said Don Saldia, the division manager with the Kalamazoo County Area Agency on Aging. "Information out there shows that some of the individuals who are more affected by these types of scams have a lot of medical bills already, or they don't have a whole lot of supports. These scammers really know that they can prey on that vulnerability to unfortunately get what they want."
 Another good bet, according to Saldia, is to look for support.
 "What we're even finding is older adults who are connected with local resources, like an area agency on aging, or a community center, or even a neighborhood association, they have more of that support," he explained. "They're more willing to go out, talk about it, and even get some information and education about what those scams look like."
 News Channel 3 asked Michigan's AARP and the Kalamazoo County Area Agency on Aging about which scams they're tracking for 2026. They include:
 An unsolicited call that asks you for your Medicare number
 An unsolicited call about your current insurance coverage
 Callers who tell you they need your information in order to send you a chip card for Medicare (Michigan's AARP says your Medicare card doesn't need a chip and will stay in its current paper version for 2027) 
 A call that tells you you now qualify for medical devices you don't currently need
 A text or call that tells you your coverage is being canceled and/or you have to pay an outstanding balance right away
 "They're good with using fear, and telling you, 'You need to do this now, and you're going to lose your benefits if you don't do this quickly,'" Pearson said.
 "People have this fear that they're going to lose their Medicare coverage," said Feuerstein-DaVita. "You have this sense of urgency and, 'Oh my gosh, something bad is going to happen if I don't respond right now."
 That fear is another common tactic scammers will use by pretending to be someone from Medicare who's calling to help you through the process.
 "You get this like relief like, 'Oh, Medicare is coming to the rescue to help me,'" said Feuerstein-DaVita. "That's a very common way how people can be victimized."
 If you ever get a call you're not sure about, the Kalamazoo County Area Agency on Aging says your local agencies are happy to help verify things.
 "I just tell folks give us call. Nothing's too small to call us about and we can verify," said Pearson.
